user:
Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters learn transferable localisation from image-level labels alone? Today they learn only from pixel masks of BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC. We replace the Dice and Focal seg_loss with a multiple-instance objective applied at all four levels to the segmentation-branch patch-to-text similarity map (mean of the top 2% patch anomaly probabilities; max and mean pooling as ablations), and train on all five source datasets with masks discarded. Primary question and hypothesis: because every patch is scored against a shared text anchor, image-level supervision aligns patch-level evidence with the text 'abnormal' direction, so the learned localisation transfers to the unseen modality and retains at least 80% of mask-supervised MVFA's pixel-level AUROC (with PRO and image AUROC also reported). A visual-only MIL control (same operator on a linear patch classifier without text anchors) tests whether text anchoring is responsible. Secondary analyses: per-level localisation quality, and a label-budget comparison on two held-out modalities between image-labelled training and mask-supervised training on 10%, 30% and 100% of the masked images.

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Two-stage anomaly-aware anchors then patch MIL, all from image labels
SUMMARY: Stage 1 learns residual text adapters that separate normal and abnormal anchors using image-level labels and an orthogonality term; stage 2 trains MVFA's segmentation adapters with top-k patch MIL against the frozen stage-1 anchors.
HYPOTHESIS: Anomaly-aware anchors learned from image labels increase held-out pixel AUROC of MIL-trained segmentation adapters by at least 2 points over frozen template anchors, and the combined method retains at least 80% of mask-supervised MVFA's pixel-AUROC margin over chance.
RESEARCH IDEA: Independent variable: anchor type during MIL (frozen template-average anchors vs. stage-1 anomaly-aware anchors). Stage 1: a residual MLP adapter on the text encoder output (ratio 0.1) trained for 10 epochs with image-level BCE on the CLS token similarity and an orthogonality penalty |cos(T_nor, T_abn)| (weight 0.1). Stage 2: seg adapters trained with top-k MIL (k = 6) and the all-patches-normal term for normal images, anchors frozen. Dependent variables: anchor separation (cosine), pixel AUROC, PRO, image AUROC on held-out modalities.
RATIONALE: Under image-level supervision, MIL localisation depends entirely on how well the text anchors separate normal and abnormal patches; MVFA's anchors are frozen template averages. Following AA-CLIP, the anchors can first be made anomaly-aware using image labels only, and patch alignment by MIL then operates against a better-separated reference.
METHOD: 1) New module text_adapter.py: TextAdapter(d=768, bottleneck=192) applied residually to the two anchor embeddings. 2) train_anchor.py (stage 1): freeze CLIP and visual adapters; optimise TextAdapter with BCE(sigmoid(t * (cos(cls, T_abn) - cos(cls, T_nor))), y) + 0.1 |cos(T_nor, T_abn)| on all source images; lr 1e-4, 10 epochs. 3) train_zero.py (stage 2): replace seg_loss with topk_mil + normal-all-patches term against stage-1 anchors; det branch unchanged. 4) Test: test_zero.py with stage-1 anchors.
EXPERIMENT: Protocol: BMAD zero-shot, leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); masks of the source datasets are discarded for all image-label-supervised variants; checkpoints selected on a validation split of the source modalities using image AUROC only (no masks used for selection); mask-supervised MVFA re-run under the same rule as the reference; 3 seeds; evaluation on the held-out modalities that have masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) for pixel metrics and on all six for image AUROC. Baselines: mask-supervised MVFA; MIL with frozen anchors; MIL with jointly (single-stage) learned anchors. Ablations: orthogonality weight; adapter bottleneck; stage-1 epochs. Metrics: anchor cosine, pixel AUROC, PRO, image AUROC. Falsification: no gain over frozen anchors.

Idea B:
TITLE: Cross-image MIL ranking for mask-free segmentation, borrowed from weakly supervised video anomaly detection
SUMMARY: Train MVFA's segmentation adapters with a ranking loss that requires the top patch scores of every abnormal image to exceed the top patch scores of normal images from the same dataset in the same mini-batch, plus sparsity and smoothness terms, using only image labels.
HYPOTHESIS: A cross-image MIL ranking loss with sparsity and smoothness yields held-out pixel AUROC at least 2 points higher than per-image top-k MIL (which only sees one image at a time, as MVFA's batch size of 1 enforces), and retains at least 80% of mask-supervised MVFA's pixel-AUROC margin over chance.
RATIONALE: Weakly supervised video anomaly detection learns to localise anomalous segments from video-level labels with a MIL ranking loss (the highest-scoring segment of an anomalous video must outrank the highest-scoring segment of a normal video), plus sparsity and temporal smoothness. Patches of an image are the spatial analogue of segments of a video. Per-image MIL, as in the parent, calibrates each image in isolation; ranking across images of the same dataset makes the scores comparable between images, which is exactly what localisation and image scoring need. MVFA's training uses batch size 1 (train_zero.py), so this requires building balanced batches.
METHOD: 1) Data loader: batches of 4 normal + 4 abnormal images from the same source dataset. 2) For level l: s_max(x) = mean of top-k patch probabilities (k = 6). Loss_rank = mean over (a, n) pairs of max(0, 1 - s_max(a) + s_max(n)). 3) Sparsity: lambda_1 * mean patch probability of abnormal images (lambda_1 = 1e-3); smoothness: lambda_2 * mean squared difference of 4-neighbour patch probabilities (lambda_2 = 1e-3). 4) Normal images: additionally all-patches-normal BCE (weight 0.5). 5) Segmentation adapters only; detection branch unchanged. 6) Code: dataset/medical_zero.py balanced sampler, loss.py mil_rank(), train_zero.py; lr 1e-4, 50 epochs.
EXPERIMENT: BMAD zero-shot leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); no source masks used by the proposed variants; checkpoints selected on source-modality validation splits by image AUROC; mask-supervised MVFA re-run under the same rule as reference; 3 seeds; pixel metrics on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC. Baselines: mask-supervised MVFA; per-image top-k MIL; asymmetric SigLIP-MIL. Ablations: k; lambda_1, lambda_2; batch composition (same dataset vs mixed). Metrics: held-out pixel AUROC, PRO, image AUROC. Falsification: no gain over per-image MIL.
